sentences.text: Scientists know Halcyornis only from a single braincase fossil discovered in the Early Eocene London Clay of southeastern England, leaving the rest of its skeleton and the front of its skull unknown.

This fossil reveals that the bird possessed large olfactory lobes relative to its forebrain and a wulst—a structure on the brain involved in vision processing—that was unusually large, comparable to that of modern parrots.
The type specimen of Halcyornis holds the distinction of being the first fossil bird ever to receive a scientific name.
Originally described in 1825 as a gull species named Larus toliapicus, it was later renamed Halcyornis by Richard Owen in 1846, a name referencing the kingfisher family.
The species belongs to the family Halcyornithidae, which includes Eocene birds found in Europe and North America and is considered to be the basal relatives of both parrots and songbirds.

Although the genus was reassigned to the family Pseudasturidae in 2007 based on skull similarities, the family Pseudasturidae is now considered a junior synonym of Halcyornithidae because Halcyornis is older than Pseudasturides.
Halcyornis lived during the Ypresian stage, between 56 and 48.07 million years ago.
